set.text: Dear Mei, thank you for the heartfelt letter you sent after the New Year dinner. I read it three times, and each time I felt a wave of nostalgia for the noisy kitchens of my own childhood. You asked why I still make dumplings by hand when the shop sells good ones. In our family it is customary for the oldest woman to fold the first dumpling of the year, and my mother did it until she was ninety. I know it sounds sentimental, but holding the dough connects me to a lineage of cooks I never met, women who fed their families through hard winters. The bamboo steamer you saw on the shelf belonged to my grandmother. I cherish it more than anything else I own. Next year, I want you beside me when I fold the first one. With love, Grandma Lin

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lineage” mean?
options: a set of old kitchen tools
the line of family members who came before her
qs.why: She means the women in her family before her, cooks she “never met.” “Her children and grandchildren” is a near miss: those come after her, not before.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “customary” mean?
options: the usual practice in the family
made to order for a customer
qs.why: Folding the first dumpling is what the family has always done, as her mother did until ninety. It is a habit, not a law.

qs.q: Why does Grandma still make dumplings by hand?
options: She cannot afford to buy dumplings.
Mei asked her to teach the skill.
It makes her feel connected to the women in her family who cooked before her.
Her doctor told her to keep her hands busy.
She wants to sell them at the market.
qs.why: She says holding the dough connects her to earlier cooks in her family. She even admits the shop sells good ones.

why: Grandma says the custom is that the oldest woman folds the first dumpling, then asks Mei (the youngest) to fold it, contradicting the custom just stated; reworded so the ending fits.

set.text: Coffee can stimulate the brain, making us feel alert and focused. The effect is useful in the morning, but it can last much longer than people expect, because the body clears caffeine slowly over several hours. A cup at four in the afternoon may leave someone only mildly alert at bedtime, yet that small effect can still delay sleep. Sleep experts warn that the losses are cumulative. Twenty minutes lost each night adds up to more than two hours over a week, and the tiredness builds. One implication of a late cup that few people consider is a tired, foggy week ahead. For anyone who struggles to rest, timing matters as much as amount. Some people try sleeping pills to induce sleep, but doctors usually suggest simpler steps first, such as a regular bedtime and a cool, dark room. It also helps to check your habits periodically, since what worked at twenty may not work at fifty.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “cumulative” mean?
qs.why: Twenty minutes a night “adds up to more than two hours over a week,” so the loss grows. “Too small to matter” is the careless reading.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “induce” mean?
qs.why: Sleeping pills are taken to make sleep happen. Coffee is what delays sleep, not the pills.

qs.q: Which statement best sums up the passage?
options: Sleeping pills are the best way to fix poor sleep.
Caffeine leaves the body within an hour.
Losing twenty minutes of sleep has no real effect.
Only people over fifty have trouble sleeping.
When you drink coffee can affect your sleep, and small nightly losses add up.
qs.why: The passage says timing matters and that small losses build over a week. It says caffeine clears slowly, over several hours, not within an hour.

why: 'implication' was used as 'the conclusion that follows' ('The implication is clear: timing matters'), not the card meaning 'a possible future effect of a decision'; rewritten so it names a future effect of a late cup.

set.text: The inaugural Riverside Jazz Festival opened last Friday with a concert in homage to Josephine Akande, the late composer whose music shaped the city's jazz scene for fifty years. The evening was led by Marcus Bell, an eminent pianist who studied with Akande as a teenager. His band, which has kept dozens of her songs in its repertoire for years, played everything from her early dance tunes to the long, slow works she wrote in her final years. Listeners could hear a three-note motif that returns again and again in her music, sometimes bright and quick, sometimes slow and sad. Bell played it with real flair, adding playful runs and sudden pauses that made the crowd laugh and cheer. Near the end, he told the audience that Akande had always said a festival was what the city needed. "Tonight," he said, "she finally has one."

qs.q: In the passage, what does “motif” mean?
options: a short musical idea that is repeated
qs.why: The three notes “return again and again” in her music. “A reason for doing something” is a motive, a different word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “inaugural” mean?
qs.why: Bell says Akande wanted a festival and “finally has one,” so this is the first. It has not been running for decades.

qs.q: Why was the evening especially meaningful, according to Bell?
options: Akande had wanted the town to have a festival, and this was the first one.
It was Bell's first time playing in public.
The festival had been held for fifty years.
Akande played piano with the band.
It raised money to clean the river.
qs.why: Akande said a festival was what the town needed, and this was the first. The fifty years refers to how long her music shaped the scene, not the festival.

why: 'repertoire' was applied to a composer's body of written works, not the card meaning (songs a person or group knows and can perform); now the band's repertoire. Also fixed 'the city's jazz scene' vs 'the river town' inconsistency.

set.text: The fire at the Dunmore storage warehouse started late on a Sunday, and by morning half the building was gone. No one was hurt, but investigators spent weeks looking for the culprit. They found it in a back room: a cheap heater left running beside a stack of cardboard boxes. The report blamed negligence rather than bad luck. Safety rules at the warehouse had grown lax over the years; fire doors were propped open, and monthly checks were often skipped. One manager who was supposed to oversee the inspections admitted that he had stopped looking closely and had begun to overlook small problems because nothing had ever gone wrong. Workers had raised concerns about the heater twice, but no one chose to heed their warnings. The company has since hired a new safety officer and installed sprinklers in every room.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “lax” mean?
qs.why: Fire doors were propped open and checks were skipped, so the rules were not followed carefully. “Far too strict” is the opposite.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “heed” mean?
options: to pay attention to and act on
qs.why: The workers warned about the heater, but no one listened and did anything about it. Hearing by accident is a near miss; the point is acting on the warning.

qs.q: Why did the manager start overlooking small problems?
options: Workers asked him to ignore them.
He was too busy fixing the heater.
The company told him to skip the checks.
He did not know how to do inspections.
Nothing had ever gone wrong before, so he stopped worrying.
The fire doors were already broken.
qs.why: He admitted he began to overlook problems “because nothing had ever gone wrong.” Workers raised concerns; they did not ask him to ignore them.

why: 'overlook small problems because nothing had ever gone wrong' reads as 'deliberately let slide' (another sense), not the card meaning 'fail to notice'; added that he stopped looking closely.

set.text: In 1912, an amateur collector named Charles Dawson announced that he had found pieces of an ancient human skull near the village of Piltdown in England. Many experts were thrilled. The bones seemed to show a missing step in human history, and museums displayed casts and replica skulls based on the find. Some scientists had doubts, because the remains did not fit well with early human fossils found in Africa and Asia. Finally, in 1953, new chemical tests showed that the find was bogus: a human skull from a much later time combined with the jaw of an orangutan, stained to look old. The teeth had even been filed down by some sly hand to look more human. Since then, many different people have been named as the hoaxer, and each new allegation has started fresh debate; a 2016 study concluded that Dawson most likely acted alone. The Piltdown hoax remains a lesson: exciting discoveries still need careful tests to validate them.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “bogus” mean?
options: fake, though made to look real
qs.why: The bones were a later skull and an ape jaw stained to look ancient. They were faked, not just damaged.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “validate” mean?
options: to explain them to the public
to confirm that they are true
qs.why: The lesson is that exciting finds must be tested to prove they are real, as the 1953 tests finally showed this one was not.

qs.q: Why did some scientists doubt the Piltdown find before 1953?
options: Chemical tests had already shown it was fake.
The bones were found by children.
It did not fit well with early human fossils found in Africa and Asia.
The skull was clearly brand new.
qs.why: The passage says the remains did not fit well with fossils from Africa and Asia. The chemical tests came only in 1953.

why: The claim that few would make 'an open allegation of fraud against respected men' before 1953 is unverifiable (early doubts were about interpretation, not fraud). Replaced with a verifiable use: many people have since been accused, and a 2016 study (De Groote et al.) concluded Dawson most likely acted alone.

set.text: To the hiring committee: I am writing to recommend Sofia Petrovic for the position of laboratory manager. Sofia worked in my lab at a reputable university research center for four years, and I can say with confidence that she is one of the finest staff members I have known. Her diligence is the first thing people notice. She labels every sample, double-checks every order, and has never missed a safety inspection. Her technical competence is equally clear; new students go to her before they come to me. I will be candid about one weakness: she can be too modest and needs encouragement to share her own ideas in meetings. But her advice has been invaluable to my team, and several of our best results grew from her suggestions. You will rarely find a candidate of her caliber. Sincerely, Professor Ahmed Karim

qs.q: In the passage, what does “candid” mean?
qs.why: He openly names a real weakness instead of hiding it. A “candid photo” is a different use of the word.

qs.q: In the passage, what does “caliber” mean?
options: the size of a gun barrel
qs.why: He means few candidates are as skilled and capable as she is. The gun-barrel meaning does not fit a person.

qs.q: What weakness does Professor Karim mention?
options: She is sometimes careless with labels.
She has missed some safety inspections.
She is not good at helping new students.
She talks too much in meetings.
She is too modest and needs encouragement to share her ideas.
qs.why: He says she “can be too modest and needs encouragement to share her own ideas.” The letter says she never missed an inspection.

why: Idea question: the correct option was the only one starting with the name 'Sofia' while the five wrong ones start 'She', a giveaway cue; made it parallel.
